rag_matches.description:
Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Tree, 5-20 m tall; outer bark minutely fissured, thin (bearing short, raised, horizontal lines on inner surface); inner bark reddish-brown on the outer edge, bearing impressed short horizontal lines, the sap with sweet, distinctive aroma; young twigs, rachises, axes of inflorescences and of leaves moderately short-appressed pubescent, glabrous in age. Leaves alternate, pinnate, mostly 8-25 cm long, essentially glabrous; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets usually alternate, often dimorphic, those of full size usually 3-5, often with 1 or 2 pairs of minute, aborted leaflets at base, rarely with 7 full-sized leaflets, the blades ± elliptic, acuminate, acute to obtuse at base, 6-16 cm long, 2.5-6(7) cm wide; major lateral veins mostly 8-12, scarcely raised below, joining before the margin, the midrib usually flat above. Panicles solitary in upper axils, 5-17 cm long; flowers greenish, mostly 5-parted; calyx bowl-shaped, shallowly lobed, 1-2 mm long, glabrate; petals ovate, 2-3 mm long, usually glabrous but with minute papillae on margin; staminal tube one-half to two-thirds as long as petals, much broader than long, moderately to sparsely pubescent outside at least toward base (often glabrous outside in South America), sparsely to densely pubescent inside; anthers twice the number of petals, slender, slightly tapered toward apex, ca 1 mm long, dehiscing along lateral margins, alternating with and ± equaling acicular lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, 1-2 mm wide, with 2 or 3 (4) locules, the trichomes dense, appressed, white on basal half; style ± equaling ovary at anthesis; stigma capitate, inconspicuously lobed, held about at height of anthers. Fruits ± globose, green at maturity, weakly verrucose, 2-3 cm diam, ± glabrous, dehiscing by 3 valves; seeds 1 or 2, covered with a shiny red aril. Rare; collected only along the shore between Bat Cove and the dock. Flowers from March to May. The fruits mature from August to September.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent, the fruits probably mature from July to October. Known only from Panama, from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Veraguas, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Colon, Chiriqui, Code, and Panama.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent.

Guavita cansa-boca, Bribri, Guava, Guava del mono Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised.

Tree, 3.5-11 (13) m tall; trunk usually 6-15 cm dbh; bark with moderately close, deep vertical fissures, but not flaking; young stems, axes of inflorescences, petioles, and underside of veins densely rufous-pubescent, the trichomes pinnately branched, often somewhat stalked. Petioles to 9 cm long; blades broadly elliptic, obtuse to abruptly short-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, 9-35 cm long, 6-18 cm wide, denticulate, the surface below canescent and completely covered with trichomes, these sessile, stellate, in part with a brown center; veins 5, dark. Panicles large, terminal, 18-22 cm long, branched many times, the branches ± flattened or angulate; flowers ± sessile; hypanthium and calyx together 1.5-2 mm long, campanulate, the teeth obscure or lacking; petals 5, white, obovate, to 1.5 mm long. Berries round to depressedglobose, to 6 mm diam, white to lavender-blue, probably becoming purple-black at full maturity; seeds numerous, minute. Croat 5693, 15070. Known only from shoreline north of the dock and south of Fairchild Point, but undoubtedly more abundant. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers at least in January, February, and May. Mature fruits have been seen in April, May, and October. Easily confused with Miconia argentea, which is similar in most respects except pubescence, trunk bark, and stature. The species ranges from Mexico to Panama and Venezuela; West Indies. In Panama, the species is known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Panama and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone.

Shrubby herb or shrub, 0.3-0.8 m; young twigs ferruginous-tomentose or ferruginous-pubescent with trichomes <0.2 mm to glabrescent. Leaves ± isomorphic; petiole 0.9-1.5 cm; blade 5.5-19 X 2.4-9.3 cm, elliptical to obovate-elliptical, cuneate at the base, acute to shortly acuminate at the tip, thin and irregularly pectinate-dentate, inconspicuously pubescent on the nerves (especially on the underside) to glabrescent, with inconspicuous punctations on the underside. Inflorescences terminal, erect, corymbose-paniculated, 2-4-pinnate, 2.8-15.2 cm, ferruginous-pubescent with trichomes <0.2 mm, the rachis usually straight, the flowers densely clustered, distributed in the distal half of the axes; peduncle absent or up to ca. 1.9 cm; bracts up to ca. 5 mm, scarious. Flowers with pedicel 4-6 mm; sepals 1.7-2.6 mm; petals purple, 2.2-3.8 mm; anthers 0.9-1.4 mm. Fruits 4-5 mm. Very wet forest, 0-900+ m; [in the vertical Caribbean Cordillera Central, in the eastern Cordillera de Talamanca (Amubri), in the Plains of Los Guatusos and San Carlos, in the Baja Talamanca, in the vertical Pacific Cordilleras de Guanacaste and Tilarán, in the northern Fila Costeña, in the protected area of Parque Nacional Carara]. Fl. Apr.-Jul. [in Mexico, Peru, and Venezuela].

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Trees, shrubs, or lianas; twigs often angled or triangularly compound in lianas, ribbed, with simple hair indumentum or rarely with spines; white sap sometimes in lianas (Serjania); stipules often present in lianas (Paullinia, Serjania), absent in tree species; tendrils (modified inflorescence) present in climbing species. Leaves compound (paripinnate, imparipinnate, trifoliate, bipinnate, bi-tri-ternate, etc.), rarely simple (Dodonaea, Llagunoa), alternate, rarely opposite or subopposite (Matayba); rachis often winged, generally with the terminal leaflet aborted in tree species, leaflets normally alternate on the rachis and with entire or serrated margins; petioles pulvinated. Inflorescences terminal, axillary, or sometimes cauliflorous, are panicles, racemes, or fascicles. Flowers generally unisexual; sepals 5-6, free or united; petals 0-5, free, sometimes with a claw; disk present; stamens (5) 8 (10), unequal, pubescent or papillose; carpels 2-3, united; ovary superior, 1-4 locular; placentation usually axillary, ovules 1-2 per locule; style 1, stigmas 2-3. Fruits are capsules, with septicidal or loculicidal dehiscence; drupes or berries, sometimes winged; seeds 1-3 per fruit, globose or flattened, sometimes arillate or with sarcotesta in dehiscent fruits.
The family consists of about 147 genera and 2215 species, mainly pantropical, with only a few genera more diverse in temperate regions, the greatest diversity is concentrated in the Neotropics and the tropics of Asia; the most diverse genera are the lianas Serjania and Paullinia; 21 genera and 90 species in CR; 7 genera and 20 species in LS.
It is recognized by its mainly compound, alternate leaves, the leaflets alternate on the rachis, with margins usually serrated and pulvinated petioles. In tree species, it is common to find at the apex of the rachis the presence of an aborted leaflet; moreover, this group lacks stipules. Stipules are present only in genera of lianas (Paullinia, Serjania, etc.). This is the only family of lianas with compound leaves, with serrated margins and milky sap. The fruits, in general, capsules with (2) 3 parts, with arillate seeds; sometimes indehiscent or drupe-like (Talisia, Sapindus), or winged and the carpels separated into 3 samaras with one seed each (Serjania, Thinouia, Dodonaea).
This family is located in the Order Sapindales, alongside families such as Meliaceae, Rutaceae, Anacardiaceae, etc. The identity of this Order is validated by recent molecular studies, which even suggest that some families considered distinct, e.g., Aceraceae, Hippocastanaceae, etc.; could be reassigned and become part of the family Sapindaceae.
Some fruit trees are directly related to the family, these include: mamón (Melicoccus), rambutan (Nephelium), akí (Bligia), etc. The fruits of Sapindus saponaria (chumino, jaboncillo) have been used as a substitute for soap. Several tree species produce good quality wood. The popular Brazilian drink called guaraná is extracted from Paullinia cupana, which is said to be the plant with the highest caffeine content (Beck, 2004).

Fruits are capsules, with septicidal or loculicidal dehiscence; drupes or berries, sometimes winged; seeds 1-3 per fruit, globose or flattened, sometimes arillate or with sarcotesta in dehiscent fruits.
The family consists of about 147 genera and 2215 species, mainly pantropical, with only a few genera more diverse in temperate regions, the greatest diversity is concentrated in the Neotropics and the tropics of Asia; the most diverse genera are the lianas Serjania and Paullinia; 21 genera and 90 species in CR; 7 genera and 20 species in LS.
It is recognized by its mainly compound, alternate leaves, the leaflets alternate on the rachis, with margins usually serrated and pulvinated petioles. In tree species, it is common to find at the apex of the rachis the presence of an aborted leaflet; moreover, this group lacks stipules. Stipules are present only in genera of lianas (Paullinia, Serjania, etc.). This is the only family of lianas with compound leaves, with serrated margins and milky sap. The fruits, in general, capsules with (2) 3 parts, with arillate seeds; sometimes indehiscent or drupe-like (Talisia, Sapindus), or winged and the carpels separated into 3 samaras with one seed each (Serjania, Thinouia, Dodonaea).
This family is located in the Order Sapindales, alongside families such as Meliaceae, Rutaceae, Anacardiaceae, etc. The identity of this Order is validated by recent molecular studies, which even suggest that some families considered distinct, e.g., Aceraceae, Hippocastanaceae, etc.; could be reassigned and become part of the family Sapindaceae.
Some fruit trees are directly related to the family, these include: mamón (Melicoccus), rambutan (Nephelium), akí (Bligia), etc. The fruits of Sapindus saponaria (chumino, jaboncillo) have been used as a substitute for soap. Several tree species produce good quality wood. The popular Brazilian drink called guaraná is extracted from Paullinia cupana, which is said to be the plant with the highest caffeine content (Beck, 2004).
